newsitem.title: USA: U.S. firms use 'no meeting' tactic in hostile deals.
newsitem.headline: U.S. firms use 'no meeting' tactic in hostile deals.

text.p: After years of rebuffing hostile takeovers with a widely-used defense known as "just say no," the new motto of some target companies is "just say no meeting."
ITT Corp., Healthdyne Technologies Inc. and ADT Ltd all recently battled hostile bidders over the timing of their annual shareholder meetings.

The shareholder session, often held in the spring, is especially important in hostile takeovers because the unwelcome bidder may try to gain control of the target by ousting its board of directors at the annual meeting.
Similarly, companies often are forced to hold special shareholder meetings to consider a hostile bid.
By delaying a shareholder meeting, a target company can pursue other plans to win shareholder support.

"This is becoming one of the key anti-takeover issues of the day," said David Drake, analyst at Institutional Shareholder Services, a Maryland-based firm that evaluates proxy fights for institutional shareholders.

Companies typically use a variety of defenses against hostile takeovers, including a "poison pill," which makes it prohibitively expensive for a potential buyer to acquire shares, a "staggered board," which prevents a buyer from ousting the entire board of directors at one time, and the "just say no" defense, in which a target company flatly rejects a bid and hopes the suitor will abandon the effort.

Experts in mergers and corporate governance say the strategy of delaying a shareholder meeting is usually effective only if the target company demonstrates it is pursuing alternatives that will benefit shareholders.

"It's not going to stave off a hostile bidder. It merely changes the timing. The company has to have a good reason why the meeting is being delayed," said John Wilcox, chairman of proxy firm Georgeson & Co.
The strategy has been critical for hotel and casino giant ITT, which is fighting a $6.5 billion hostile bid from rival Hilton Hotels Corp.
Although it typically holds its annual meeting in May, ITT has not yet scheduled the annual session and is concentrating on divesting non-core assets in an effort to thwart Hilton's bid.
Hilton filed suit to force ITT to hold a meeting in mid-May, but a U.S. judge last month upheld ITT's position.
"At some point, there is a judgement day and we'll be there when that judgement day occurs," said Hilton spokesman Marc Grossman.

ITT officials declined to comment on its defense, but two sources close to the company said it was crucial to delay the meeting. It has until as late as mid-November to hold the shareholder gathering.
The company, which already has announced plans to divest some assets, hopes to sell more by autumn in order to boost its stock price and keep shareholders from being lured by the Hilton bid.
The tactic used by ITT "is being recognized as OK because it's really being done for legitimate purposes," said one person familiar with the company's methods.
The strategy also has been used by Healthdyne Technologies in its attempt to fend off a $173 million takeover by Invacare Corp.

Although Invacare initially sought a court order for a meeting by June 30, Healthdyne prevailed in its plan to hold a meeting July 30 -- so investors could assess second-quarter results before voting on the hostile bid.

"When you're defending a takeover, time is your friend. Everything is about buying time to pursue alternatives," said Wilder Fulford, a Salomon Brothers investment banker who is representing Invacare and has been involved in other hostile transactions.
Western Resources Inc. tried unsuccessfully to force electronic security giant ADT to hold a meeting in June to consider its unsolicited $3.5 billion offer.
ADT, which rejected the offer and then struck a $5.4 billion pact with Tyco International Ltd, plans a July 8 meeting of shareholders to consider Western's effort to oust the board.
So far, however, the strategy has not weakened the resolve of hostile bidders, who vow to let shareholders decide who should own the company.
"You can run, but you can't hide," Fulford said. "Sooner or later, the shareholders will have their say."
